newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH OPPOSTION BLASTS EX-COMMUNISTS IN TV DEBATE.
newsitem.headline: POLISH OPPOSTION BLASTS EX-COMMUNISTS IN TV DEBATE.

text.p: Poland's major opposition party, the Union for Freedom, blasted the co-ruling ex-communists over economic policies in a television debate, defying speculations that the two parties may join forces after the coming elections.

The Union's leader Leszek Balcerowicz urged groups rooted in the Solidarity movement, which defeated the communist rule in 1989, to unite after the polls to speed up market reforms, which he said the ex-communists had slowed down.

"I treat it as my mission... to create a great coalition which would complete the reconstruction of Poland," Balcerowicz said during the nationally televised debate with Jozef Oleksy, leader of the ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD).

The debate was a prelude to the campaign for parliamentary elections, due around September this year, which will pit the SLD, in power since 1993 along with a peasant party, against the Solidarity-rooted groups.

Balcerowicz said the new coalition should speed up the liberalisation and demonopolisation of the economy, hand over more powers to local government and launch vital reforms of the social security and education systems, which the current government had failed to implement.
Oleksy defended the ruling coalition's score, saying the economy was on the growth track, inflation was falling and real wages rising.

But Balcerowicz, one of authors of Poland economic "shock therapy" after 1989, said the achievements could have been more spectacular and sustainable had policies during the last four years been more market oriented.
"The SLD consumed fruits of past efforts and did not sow grains for future harvest," he said.
But Balcerowicz said he feared it might be difficut to put together a coalition of Solidarity-rooted parties that would implement clear pro-reform policies.

He criticised the strongest of these groups -- the Solidarity Electoral Action (AWS), a bloc of the Solidarity trade union and about 30 small rightist parties -- for courting the right-radical Movement for Poland's Reconstruction (ROP) into an alliance and neglecting cooperation with the Union.
He said the coalition between the AWS and the ROP, which he said advocated populist policies, would be harmful for the economy and Poland's plans to join the European Union.
Recent opinion polls have given the ex-communist and the AWS between 20 and 30 percent support, with other parties trailing far behind.
But analysts say lower-rated parties, such as the Peasant Party, the ROP and the Union for Freedom, may hold the balance of power in the next parliament. -- Warsaw Newsroom +48 22 653 9700
